findings.explanation: SOA Expire is 30 minutes (1800s). RFC 1912 §2.2 recommends 1,209,600–2,419,200 seconds (14–28 days). If the primary nameserver becomes unreachable, secondary nameservers will stop serving this zone after only 30 minutes (1800s).

If Expire is not greater than Refresh + Retry, secondary nameservers may stop serving the zone before they've had a chance to retry the primary.

traffic_engineering.explanation: This domain uses short TTLs across 4 record types (A record at 42s), consistent with DNS-based traffic management (GSLB). Enterprises operating large anycast networks intentionally use short TTLs to enable rapid failover, geographic steering, and load distribution. This is a deliberate infrastructure choice, not a misconfiguration. RFC 1035 §3.2.1 permits any TTL value the zone administrator selects. The findings below reflect deviation from typical values for reference, not necessarily actionable recommendations for this class of infrastructure.

entries.propagation_note: A records typically propagate within 5 minutes. Some resolvers may cache up to the TTL value.
AAAA records follow the same propagation pattern as A records.
MX record changes may take up to 1 hour to propagate. Mail delivery may be affected during transition.
TXT records (including SPF) typically propagate within 1 hour. Verify with multiple resolvers.
Nameserver changes can take 24–48 hours for full global propagation due to parent zone TTLs.
CNAME changes propagate quickly but downstream records inherit the CNAME TTL.
CAA record changes take effect within TTL. Certificate authorities check at issuance time.
SOA changes propagate to secondaries based on the Refresh interval in the SOA record.
SPF record changes propagate within the TXT record TTL. Test with dig before relying on scan results.
DMARC policy changes at _dmarc subdomain propagate within TTL. Reporting changes take 24–48h to reflect in aggregate reports.
DKIM selector records propagate within TTL. New selectors are available immediately once published; key rotation requires overlap period.
MTA-STS policy changes require updating both the DNS TXT record AND the policy file at /.well-known/mta-sts.txt. The max_age directive in the policy controls how long senders cache it.
TLS-RPT changes propagate within TTL. Report delivery changes take effect in the next reporting period (typically 24 hours).
BIMI record changes propagate within TTL. VMC certificate validation by mail providers may take additional time.
TLSA/DANE records must be published BEFORE rotating TLS certificates. Premature certificate rotation breaks DANE validation.
DNSSEC signing changes (DS record updates at registrar) can take 24–48 hours. Key rollovers require careful timing per RFC 7583.
DANE/TLSA record updates follow the TLSA TTL. Coordinate with TLS certificate lifecycle.

results.title: DNSSEC Authentication
results.fail_explanation: DNSSEC not authenticated — DNS responses for this domain are not cryptographically validated. An attacker positioned between the resolver and authoritative server can forge responses (Kaminsky attack, RFC 5452). Per RFC 4033 §2, "DNSSEC provides origin authentication and integrity assurance."

weakness_refs.mapping_rationale: Absent DNSSEC means resolvers cannot verify the authenticity of DNS data (CWE-345), exposing the resolution path to on-path forgery (CWE-300) and cache poisoning (CAPEC-142/141). Mapping verified against MITRE CWE/CAPEC and Bugcrowd VRT.

results.title: DNSSEC Chain of Trust Validated
results.fail_explanation: DNSSEC chain of trust not validated. Per RFC 4035 §5, validators must be able to trace a chain of signed DNSKEY and DS records from a trust anchor to the zone. The AD (Authenticated Data) flag was not set by the validating resolver.

weakness_refs.mapping_rationale: A broken or unvalidated chain of trust leaves DNS answers unauthenticated (CWE-345), the precondition for DNS cache poisoning (CAPEC-142). Mapping verified against MITRE CWE/CAPEC and Bugcrowd VRT.

results.title: DNSSEC Key Rollover Readiness
results.fail_explanation: No CDS/CDNSKEY automation — DNSSEC key rollover requires manual registrar coordination. Per RFC 8078, CDS and CDNSKEY records enable automated, authenticated DS updates at the parent.

weakness_refs.mapping_rationale: Permissive SPF without DMARC enforcement lets a forged sender bypass origin authentication (CWE-290) by faking the source domain (CAPEC-194/151). SPF is contributory, so confidence is medium; VRT files this failure mode under the DMARC entry. CWE/CAPEC verified against MITRE.

p=none and p=quarantine do not instruct receivers to reject unauthenticated mail, so sender authentication is effectively bypassed (CWE-290), enabling domain identity spoofing (CAPEC-151), forged-source mail (CAPEC-194) and spear phishing (CAPEC-163). This is the flagship false-green-checkmark gap: tools mark DMARC present as compliant while the domain remains spoofable. Mapping verified against MITRE CWE/CAPEC and Bugcrowd VRT.

results.title: DKIM Signature Availability
results.fail_explanation: DKIM not discoverable for this mail-sending domain. Per RFC 6376, DKIM provides cryptographic proof of message origin. Without DKIM, email from this domain cannot be cryptographically verified by receivers.

results.title: DANE / TLSA Deployment
results.fail_explanation: DANE/TLSA not deployed. Per RFC 6698, DANE binds TLS server certificates to DNS names using DNSSEC, providing authentication independent of the Certificate Authority system.

results.title: BIMI Brand Indicator
results.fail_explanation: BIMI not configured or logo invalid. BIMI requires DMARC p=reject and a valid SVG logo to display brand indicators in supporting email clients.

weakness_refs.mapping_rationale: Dangling records pointing to unclaimed infrastructure are the direct precondition for subdomain takeover. Bugcrowd VRT classifies this explicitly; no single authoritative CWE/CAPEC ID is cited to avoid an unverified mapping.

results.title: DNS Delegation Consistency
results.fail_explanation: DNS delegation inconsistency detected. Parent and child zone NS records, glue records, or SOA serials do not agree. This can cause intermittent resolution failures and makes the zone vulnerable to hijacking.
